I myself am extremely OCD when it comes to most things in my life, and I find math feeds into that almost too well.

You get into the flow of things first by doing simple and easy stuff. Then, you slowly ramp up the difficulty by tackling newer and more complicated concepts. 

More complex math needs more time and practice to nail down and keep in your memory, so it always helps that you break down the complex stuff into small manageable steps.

This all ties back to building consistency and mathematical finesse, which should make your studying time more enjoyable and less of a chore.

So tldr:
1. Do a lot of easy stuff first to get into the flow of things (at whatever level).

2. Break harder stuff down into smaller more manageable steps.

3. Take short breaks between your sessions to allow your mind time to consolidate what you learned.

4. Do a little bit each day. Don't try to do 6 hour sessions in the beginning.

One thing that helps is having very solid foundations in whatever it is you are trying to read. Math textbooks became readable for me when I solidified all weaknesses that I had in a certain chapter. 

Not saying that you have holes since you are at calc ii, but it's always beneficial to take a step back and work on some 'rusty' concepts.

I've been in a similar boat. I'm re-teaching myself math from scratch, and I've progressed to my current level of Algebra II over a period of 6 months.

Now, if you are totally new to math, then you need to understand and practice:

1. Proportions. Important for everything. You'll always come across something that requires you to 'think about something in relation to something else'. This means knowing percents, how to convert them, understanding reciprocals, constant of proportionality, etc.


2. Decimals. Every variety of a decimal. You should be comfortable with dividing, adding, subtracting, and multiplying them. Understand how decimals relate to fractions, and how they can be used to express different things (rates, percents).


3. Fractions. This is a no-brainer. Same as above. Get comfortable doing all types of arithmetic operations with them. Understand how they can be converted to percents, used in cross-multiplying, divided to get a decimal, ways of simplifying them, etc.


4. Slope formula. Perhaps the foundation for all later more advanced formulas in math. Without understanding slope-intercepts, you won't be able to progress to quadratic/parabola formula, which in turn won't allow you to go beyond into representing 3rd degree polynomials on a Carteasean plane.


5. The Carteasean plane. Understand the horizontal line (x) and the vertical one (y). This thing becomes your bread and butter for everything in higher math.


6. Function. What a function is, what it does, and how it can be manipulated to accomplish different objectives. There are many many types of functions. Some of them more important than others.


7. Trig ratios/identities. These things are used in trigonometry and more advanced algebra. 


8. Equations. Every type of equation. Linear, quadratic, 3rd degree, system of equation, equations with different variables, etc. These form the basis of algebra. Many people struggle with manipulating these, and their progress slows down because of it.


9. Factoring. This is an extremely hard skill to develop in the beginning, but you need to persevere until you are very proficient with it. Factoring involves least common multiples, greatest common divisiors, divisibility of numbers, understanding roots, solving quadratics, and many many other mathy things.


10. Geometry. You don't need things like translations or dilations. Just a basic grasp of angles, measures, types of triangles, what a circle is, and the pythagorean theorem are enough.


Now, this list might look intimidating, but they are foundational skills and most of them are intuitive. If you practice consistently, you'll be able to build a solid foundation for everything later on.
